nodes.text: Important Tax Dates & Deadlines in Australia — 2026 Guide

nodes.html: Missing a tax deadline rarely causes an immediate crisis — but the penalties, interest and default assessments that follow are entirely avoidable when you know the dates that apply to you. This guide brings together the key Australian tax deadlines for individuals, businesses, BAS lodgers, superannuation and companies or trusts in one place, updated for the 2026 financial year. Check what applies to you, then get matched with a vetted local accountant who can keep you on time.

nodes.html: If you lodge your own individual tax return, the deadline is 31 October each year. If you use a registered tax agent, you generally receive an extended lodgement deadline — often as late as May the following year, provided you are on the agent's lodgement program before 31 October. That extended deadline is one of the clearest reasons to engage an agent rather than self-lodge. Late lodgement can trigger a failure-to-lodge (FTL) penalty and, where tax is payable, general interest charge (GIC) on the outstanding amount.

nodes.html: If you are registered for GST, you lodge a Business Activity Statement (BAS). Quarterly BAS is generally due on the 28th of the month after the quarter ends — so 28 July, 28 October, 28 January and 28 April. Monthly BAS is due on the 21st of the following month. Registered agents often receive extended BAS lodgement dates. PAYG instalments and income tax instalments are reported through the BAS as well. Late BAS attracts FTL penalties and interest on any net amount payable.

nodes.html: With the introduction of Payday Super from 1 July 2026, employers must pay super guarantee each payday. The contributions must reach the employee's super fund within 7 business days of payday. For SMSF members, personal contributions must be received by 28 January and 28 July to count toward each half-year's cap. Missing SG deadlines triggers the super guarantee charge (SGC) and, for company directors, personal director penalty notices.

nodes.html: Companies, trusts and partnerships lodge their own tax returns, separate from the individuals behind them. Company and trust returns are generally due by 15 January (or later if a registered agent lodges on your behalf). Trust distribution resolutions should be made by 30 June each year — before year-end — to be valid. Companies also face ASIC annual review fees and lodgement deadlines. Directors remain personally liable for unpaid PAYG withholding and super guarantee, so staying on time matters.

nodes.html: A number of tax-effective moves must happen before 30 June to count in the current financial year: making super contributions within your cap, pre-paying expenses, writing off obsolete stock, settling bad debts, and documenting trust distribution resolutions. After 30 June those opportunities close for that year. A matched accountant reviews your position in May or June and flags the actions worth taking before year-end — proactive planning that reduces tax rather than reacting after the fact.
